parts: Lesson 4: Methods of Cooking Food — Summary

Cooking makes food easy to digest; improves appearance, texture, colour, flavour and taste (acceptability); adds variety to meals; helps keep food longer (boiled milk, chapatti versus dough); and makes food safe by killing harmful micro-organisms. Pasteurisation heats milk to a high temperature and cools it quickly to destroy micro-organisms. Animal foods (meat, fish, eggs) must be cooked thoroughly, and cooked food should not be left over two hours at room temperature in summer.

Moist heat: boiling, simmering/stewing, steaming, pressure cooking. Dry heat: baking, roasting, grilling (200–300 degrees C, crisp texture and brown colour). Frying in oil or ghee: deep frying and shallow frying. Other methods: microwave and solar cooking.

Boiling cooks food in enough water; wash first, boil the water first, cover the food and use a lid, do not overcook, boil potatoes with skin; use the water for soup or gravy. Advantage: safe, simple, suits large-scale cooking; disadvantage: water-soluble nutrients are lost if the water is thrown. Stewing (simmering) cooks in a small quantity of water below boiling point for a long time; juices and nutrients are retained but it takes longer. Steaming cooks with the heat of water vapour (steamer, idli maker; idli, dhokla, momos); it is quick, conserves nutrients, colour and flavour and gives light food good for the sick, elderly and children. Pressure cooking uses steam under pressure above 100 degrees C; food cooks in about one-third the time, all bacteria are killed, fuel is saved and little water is needed; keep the weight vent and gasket clean.

Baking cooks in a heated closed oven (bread, cakes, biscuits); roasting is cooking directly on a hot tava, sand or fire (brinjal, maize, groundnuts, papad); grilling uses an iron grid over a glowing fire or between heated bars, slower than roasting (kababs, bati). Shallow frying uses a little oil (paratha, tikki); deep frying immerses the food in hot oil (pakora, puri, samosa). Fried food keeps longer but is difficult to digest and high in calories. Precautions: even pieces, heat oil well then lower heat, a few pieces at a time, drain on absorbent paper, strain and store used oil, avoid repeated heating. Microwave cooking is quick but needs electricity and may dry food. Solar cooking has no smoke or running cost and is eco-friendly but needs sunshine.

Vitamin A is oxidised in an open pan and destroyed by very hot oil (about 300 degrees C); cook in a covered pan. Vitamin B complex dissolves in washing and cooking water and is lost with cooking soda; riboflavin in milk is destroyed by sunlight. Vitamin C is destroyed by heat and oxidation, long exposure after cutting, washing after cutting, fine cutting, soda and discarded water. Proteins coagulate; overheating makes them dry, rubbery and hard to digest; acids toughen them (add at the end); protein and sugar cooked long (kheer) brown and lose quality. Oils and fats deteriorate when heated repeatedly. Minerals are lost when cooking water is thrown away.

Wash vegetables before cutting; scrape peels thin; cut into large pieces just before cooking; put into boiling water; use just enough water and do not throw it away; no cooking soda; tamarind or lemon juice helps conserve vitamins; cook rice in water that is fully absorbed; use a covered pan with a well-fitting lid; do not overcook; prefer the fastest method.

Enrichment or enhancement improves the nutrients of foods by simple, low-cost methods. Combination: eat foods of different groups together (rice with dal, khichri, missi roti, dhokla); pulses supply the amino acids cereals lack, so the protein becomes as good as milk protein. Fermentation: micro-organisms (curd, yeast or natural) change nutrients into simpler and better forms and create vitamin B complex and C; foods become soft and digestible (curd, idli, dhokla, bread, bhatura). Germination: soak grains 8–16 hours and sprout 12–24 hours in a moist cloth; digestibility and vitamins rise at no extra cost.
